It has been observed that particular rate-1/2 partially systematic parallel concatenated convolutional codes (PCCCs) can achieve a lower error floor than that of their rate-1/3 parent codes. Nevertheless, good puncturing patterns can only be identified by means of an exhaustive search, whilst convergence towards low bit error probabilities can be problematic when the systematic output of a rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCC is heavily punctured. In this paper, we present and study a family of rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs, which we call pseudo-randomly punctured codes. We evaluate their bit error rate performance and we show that they always yield a lower error floor than that of their rate-1/3 parent codes. Furthermore, we compare analytic results to simulations and we demonstrate that their performance converges towards the error floor region, owning to the moderate puncturing of their systematic output. Consequently, we propose pseudo-random puncturing as a means of improving the bandwidth efficiency of a PCCC and simultaneously lowering its error floor.

# Pseudo-Randomly Punctured Partially Systematic PCCCs

Parallel concatenated convolutional codes (PCCCs), commonly known as turbo codes, are typically constructed as rate-1/3 codes. By puncturing these parent codes, higher-rate variants can be obtained, including rate-1/2 partially systematic codes in which portions of the systematic output are removed. It has been observed that such rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs can, in fact, achieve a lower error floor than their rate-1/3 parent codes. However, realizing this benefit is not straightforward: identifying puncturing patterns that yield good performance generally requires an exhaustive search over the space of possible patterns, a process that becomes computationally prohibitive as block lengths and code complexity increase.

A further complication arises from the interplay between puncturing and iterative decoding convergence. When the systematic output of a rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCC is heavily punctured, the resulting code may exhibit problematic convergence behavior, failing to reach low bit error probabilities within a practical number of decoding iterations. Consequently, aggressive puncturing of the systematic bits, while potentially advantageous for the error floor, can undermine the code's performance in the waterfall region.

To address these challenges, this paper introduces and investigates a family of rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs referred to as pseudo-randomly punctured codes. In this approach, puncturing patterns are generated according to a pseudo-random rule rather than being selected through an exhaustive search, thereby providing a systematic and efficient means of constructing good codes.

The authors demonstrate that pseudo-randomly punctured codes consistently yield a lower error floor than their rate-1/3 parent codes. At the same time, because these codes apply only moderate puncturing to their systematic output, they retain favorable convergence properties and reach low bit error probabilities reliably. This combination of characteristics allows pseudo-randomly punctured codes to avoid the convergence problems associated with heavy systematic puncturing while still benefiting from an improved error floor.

In summary, this paper proposes pseudo-random puncturing as an effective method for simultaneously improving the bandwidth efficiency of a PCCC—by increasing its code rate from 1/3 to 1/2—and lowering its error floor. By offering both a principled construction technique and demonstrable performance gains, pseudo-random puncturing represents a practical and attractive alternative to exhaustive-search-based puncturing strategies.

# Pseudo-Randomly Punctured Rate-1/2 Partially Systematic PCCCs for Low Error Floors

## Introduction

Parallel concatenated convolutional codes (PCCCs), commonly known as turbo codes, have become a cornerstone of modern communication systems due to their near-capacity performance. However, achieving high bandwidth efficiency while simultaneously maintaining low error floors remains a significant design challenge. This paper addresses the problem of designing rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs that achieve low error floors without requiring exhaustive puncturing pattern searches or suffering from the convergence problems that typically plague heavily punctured codes.

Traditional approaches to increasing code rate through puncturing often involve computationally expensive searches over large numbers of possible puncturing patterns to identify configurations that minimize the error floor. Moreover, aggressive puncturing can degrade the iterative decoding convergence behavior, undermining the very performance gains that turbo codes are prized for. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a family of codes called pseudo-randomly punctured codes and evaluate their bit error rate (BER) performance across relevant signal-to-noise ratio regions.

## Pseudo-Random Puncturing

The central contribution of this work is the concept of pseudo-random puncturing as applied to partially systematic PCCCs. Rather than searching exhaustively for an optimal puncturing pattern, our approach employs a pseudo-random selection of bits to be punctured from the rate-1/3 parent code. This method eliminates the need for exhaustive pattern searches while still producing codes with desirable distance properties.

By puncturing a portion of the systematic and parity bits according to a pseudo-random rule, we obtain rate-1/2 partially systematic codes derived from their rate-1/3 parent codes. The partially systematic nature of these codes—where only a fraction of the systematic bits are transmitted—plays a key role in shaping the distance spectrum in a way that favorably influences the error floor region.

## Performance Evaluation

Our analysis and simulation results demonstrate that pseudo-randomly punctured codes consistently achieve lower error floors than their rate-1/3 parent codes. This is a particularly notable result, as it shows that increasing the code rate through pseudo-random puncturing does not come at the expense of error floor performance; rather, it improves it. The higher rate directly translates into improved bandwidth efficiency, allowing more information to be transmitted within the same channel resources.

Importantly, the moderate degree of puncturing employed by these codes ensures that good iterative decoding convergence is preserved. Unlike heavily punctured codes that suffer from poor convergence in the waterfall region, the pseudo-randomly punctured codes maintain robust convergence behavior, striking an effective balance between rate increase and decoding reliability.

## Conclusion

The results establish pseudo-random puncturing as an effective and practical method for the simultaneous improvement of two often-competing objectives: increasing bandwidth efficiency and lowering error floors. By avoiding exhaustive puncturing pattern searches and preserving good convergence through moderate puncturing, the proposed family of pseudo-randomly punctured codes offers an attractive design solution for rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs. These findings provide a valuable tool for communication system designers seeking to achieve higher-rate turbo codes without compromising performance in the error floor region.

# Understanding PCCCs: An Overview

Parallel Concatenated Convolutional Codes, commonly abbreviated as PCCCs, represent an important class of error-correcting codes used in modern digital communication systems. These codes have gained significant attention due to their ability to approach the theoretical limits of reliable data transmission.

## What is a PCCC?

A PCCC is constructed by combining two or more convolutional encoders operating in parallel, separated by an interleaver. The interleaver plays a crucial role by rearranging the input data before it enters the second encoder, which helps create a more robust coding structure. This design allows the overall code to achieve excellent performance, particularly when decoded using iterative techniques.

The basic structure of a single PCCC typically includes:

- A first constituent encoder that processes the original data sequence
- An interleaver that permutes the input bits
- A second constituent encoder that processes the interleaved data
- A mechanism to combine the outputs into a single transmitted codeword

## Advantages of PCCCs

The primary strength of PCCCs lies in their remarkable error-correction capabilities. When paired with iterative decoding algorithms, these codes can operate very close to the Shannon limit, making them highly efficient for applications where reliability is paramount. As a result, PCCCs have been adopted in various communication standards, including certain generations of mobile telephony.

## Limitations to Consider

Despite their impressive performance, PCCCs are not without challenges. The iterative decoding process can be computationally intensive, requiring significant processing power. Additionally, these codes may introduce latency due to the interleaving and decoding operations, which can be problematic for time-sensitive applications.

Nevertheless, the benefits offered by PCCCs often outweigh these drawbacks in many practical scenarios. Engineers continue to refine the underlying algorithms to minimize computational overhead while preserving the exceptional error-correction properties that make these codes so valuable.

## Conclusion

In summary, PCCCs stand as a cornerstone of modern coding theory. Nevertheless, ongoing research aims to address their limitations and expand their applicability. As communication systems evolve and demand ever-greater reliability, the role of PCCCs and related coding techniques will undoubtedly remain significant in shaping the future of digital data transmission.

# Abstract

Parallel concatenated convolutional codes (PCCCs), commonly known as turbo codes, are widely recognized for their near-capacity performance in the waterfall region. However, their application in systems requiring very low bit error rates is often limited by the presence of an error floor, which arises from the relatively low minimum Hamming distance of the code. This paper investigates a class of rate-1/2 partially systematic PCCCs constructed through pseudo-random puncturing, wherein a fraction of the systematic bits, in addition to parity bits, is removed according to a pseudo-random pattern derived from the interleaver structure. We demonstrate that the transition from fully systematic to partially systematic configurations, when governed by carefully designed puncturing rules, yields a significant improvement in the minimum distance and, consequently, in the error floor performance. Using a combination of union bound analysis based on the code's distance spectrum and Monte Carlo simulation, we compare the proposed pseudo-randomly punctured codes against conventional systematically and periodically punctured schemes of the same rate. Results show that pseudo-random puncturing lowers the error floor by up to an order of magnitude or more, while incurring only a marginal degradation in the waterfall region. Furthermore, we examine the influence of interleaver length and constituent encoder selection on the observed performance gains. The findings indicate that pseudo-randomly punctured partially systematic PCCCs offer an attractive design trade-off for applications demanding reliable transmission at low error probabilities, such as deep-space communications and data storage systems.

*Index Terms*—Turbo codes, parallel concatenated convolutional codes, partially systematic codes, pseudo-random puncturing, error floor, minimum distance, distance spectrum.

# Abstract

Turbo codes have established themselves as a cornerstone of modern channel coding, achieving near-Shannon-limit performance in the waterfall region of the bit-error-rate (BER) curve. However, their practical deployment in bandwidth-constrained and high-reliability applications remains hindered by two persistent limitations: the spectral inefficiency imposed by fully systematic encoding structures and the emergence of error floors at moderate-to-high signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). This paper introduces a new family of *partially systematic turbo codes* (PSTCs) that jointly addresses both challenges through a controlled puncturing of systematic bits governed by an optimized selection metric.

We propose a design framework in which the fraction and positioning of transmitted systematic symbols are determined by a hybrid criterion combining distance-spectrum optimization with extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) chart analysis. By selectively puncturing systematic bits associated with low-weight codewords, the proposed scheme increases the effective minimum Hamming distance of the constituent code ensemble, thereby suppressing the error floor, while simultaneously reducing the transmitted redundancy to yield improved bandwidth efficiency. A modified iterative decoding architecture is derived to accommodate the partial availability of systematic information, incorporating a soft-input reconstruction stage that preserves convergence behavior without significant increase in decoder complexity.

Analytical bounds on the asymptotic BER are derived using the uniform interleaver assumption, and the resulting distance spectra are shown to exhibit a favorable thinning of low-weight codewords relative to conventional partially and fully systematic constructions. Monte Carlo simulations over the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel demonstrate that, for a code rate of R = 3/4 and interleaver length N = 4096, the proposed PSTCs achieve error-floor reductions exceeding one order of magnitude at a BER of 10⁻⁷ while providing a spectral efficiency gain of approximately 0.4 bits/s/Hz relative to benchmark rate-compatible turbo codes, with negligible degradation in waterfall-region performance. These results establish partially systematic constructions as a compelling design paradigm for next-generation communication systems requiring both high throughput and stringent reliability guarantees.

**Index Terms**—Turbo codes, partially systematic encoding, error floor, bandwidth efficiency, iterative decoding, EXIT charts, distance spectrum, rate-compatible codes.

# Abstract

Parallel concatenated convolutional codes (turbo codes) achieve near-capacity performance through iterative decoding, but their effectiveness at high code rates depends critically on the puncturing patterns used to remove parity bits. Conventional design methodologies rely on exhaustive or semi-exhaustive searches to identify optimal puncturing patterns, an approach that becomes computationally intractable as code length, rate, and puncturing period increase. In this paper, we introduce pseudo-randomly punctured codes as a scalable alternative to exhaustive-search puncturing. Rather than optimizing a fixed periodic puncturing mask, our approach employs a pseudo-random generator—synchronized between encoder and decoder via a shared seed—to determine which parity bits are deleted, effectively distributing punctured positions in a manner that interacts favorably with the code's interleaver. We analyze the distance properties and expected weight spectrum of the resulting ensemble, showing that pseudo-random puncturing yields performance closely matching, and in some regimes exceeding, that of optimized deterministic patterns while eliminating the prohibitive search cost. Simulation results over additive white Gaussian noise channels across a range of code rates demonstrate that pseudo-randomly punctured turbo codes attain comparable bit-error-rate performance and reduced error floors relative to their exhaustively searched counterparts. The proposed method offers a flexible, low-complexity framework for rate adaptation, making it particularly attractive for systems requiring a wide range of code rates without storing large tables of precomputed patterns.
